name: Aeneid
kicker: Virgil’s Roman epic · Rome’s own foundation myth
briefing: After the Trojan War, a Trojan prince flees burning Troy carrying his father on his back, determined to find his people a new home. Blown off course to Carthage, he falls for Queen Dido before duty forces him onward to Italy, where his descendants will found Rome. Commissioned to give Rome its own epic to rival Homer’s, Virgil was still revising _the Aeneid_ when he died.

qb.tip: Only one Middle School/Easy High School tossup came up, so this sample leans on 10 Regular High School tossups too; one of the eleven is actually a tossup on “Aeneas” that simply accepts “The Aeneid” as an alternate answer.

sample.note: the 1 real Middle School/Easy High School tossup plus 10 Regular High School tossups for this answer line (power-marked); one of the eleven is an “Aeneas” tossup that also accepts “The Aeneid”

tossups.p: A Harpy named Celaeno curses this poem’s wandering travelers, warning that they will not found their city until hunger forces them to eat their own “tables.” Earlier, the priest Laocoon is killed by sea serpents after warning the Trojans not to trust a certain wooden horse.
tossups.r: This poem’s hero later visits the future site of Rome and receives a shield made by the god Vulcan showing the future Battle of Actium. For 10 points, name this Latin epic by Virgil about a Trojan prince’s journey to found Rome.

tossups.p: This poem’s hero loses his wife Creusa while fleeing burning Troy with his father on his back and his son at his side. Her ghost later appears to tell him to sail on without her.
tossups.r: Guided by the Sibyl of Cumae and a golden bough, this poem’s hero travels to the underworld in Book Six, where his father’s spirit previews the future glory of Rome. For 10 points, name this epic poem by Virgil.

tossups.p: During a royal hunt, a storm sent by Juno drives this poem’s hero into a cave with the Carthaginian queen he will later abandon. That queen, a widow of Sychaeus [“sih-KEE-us”], had fled to Africa and founded Carthage after her own brother Pygmalion murdered her husband.
tossups.r: Betrayed and heartbroken, that queen stabs herself with the hero’s own sword atop a funeral pyre. For 10 points, name this epic poem in which Dido falls in love with the title Trojan prince, written by Virgil.

tossups.p: This poem opens with the goddess Juno still furious over an old insult to her beauty, so she sends a storm to wreck this poem’s hero’s fleet near Carthage. In the underworld, this poem’s hero later meets the ghost of his helmsman Palinurus, who fell overboard while asleep at the rudder.
tossups.r: This poem begins, “I sing of arms and the man.” For 10 points, name this Roman epic about the journey of a Trojan refugee, written by Virgil.

tossups.p: In Book Two of this poem, the Greek spy Sinon convinces the Trojans to drag a massive wooden horse inside their walls, leading to the city’s fall. This poem’s hero then carries his father Anchises [“an-KY-seez”] out of the city on his back, losing his wife Creusa in the chaos.
tossups.r: That hero later fights Turnus, the king of the Rutulians, for the hand of the princess Lavinia. For 10 points, name this Roman epic, written by Virgil, that ends with its hero defeating Turnus.

tossups.p: This poem’s hero descends to the underworld and exits through the Gate of Ivory, reserved for false dreams, rather than the Gate of Horn. In an earlier book, he holds funeral games in Sicily to honor his dead father, during which despairing Trojan women try to burn his fleet.
tossups.r: This poem’s hero is the son of Venus and the mortal Anchises. For 10 points, name this epic poem by Virgil about the journey of this hero, a Trojan prince who becomes an ancestor of the Romans.

tossups.p: In this poem, the warrior maiden Camilla is killed by the warrior Arruns [“AR-unz”], who is then struck down by an arrow sent by the goddess Diana’s companion Opis. This poem’s hero kills Turnus in a rage after recognizing the belt of his slain ally Pallas.
tossups.r: At a temple in Carthage, this poem’s hero also sees a mural depicting the Trojan War, the first of several famous ekphrases [“EK-fruh-seez”] in the poem. For 10 points, name this Roman epic by Virgil.

tossups.p: Turnus’s sister Juturna [“yoo-TUR-na”] disguises herself as a charioteer to protect her brother from the single combat that ends this poem. Earlier, the son of this poem’s hero shoots a tame stag while hunting, sparking a war in Italy.
tossups.r: This poem’s hero abandons Dido, the queen of Carthage, to continue his voyage toward Italy. For 10 points, name this epic in which a Trojan prince’s descendants go on to found Rome, written by Virgil.

tossups.p: Virgil was reportedly still revising this poem when he died, having modeled it on Homer’s epics to glorify the new Roman emperor Augustus. A Harpy named Celaeno predicts that this poem’s travelers will found their city only after they are forced to eat bread used as tables.
tossups.r: This poem’s hero loses his wife Creusa while escaping the burning city of Troy. For 10 points, name this Latin epic about a Trojan refugee who becomes the ancestor of the Romans.

tossups.p: This poem contains an extended simile comparing the builders of a great city to bees at work in a hive. Its hero is guided by the Sibyl of Cumae and a golden bough into the underworld, where he glimpses the future heroes of Rome.
tossups.r: A storm sent by Juno first drives this poem’s hero to Carthage, where Queen Dido falls in love with him. For 10 points, name this epic poem by Virgil, which ends with its hero’s defeat of Turnus.

tossups.p: This poem’s hero’s fleet is wrecked by a storm after Juno bribes the wind god Aeolus with the promise of a nymph bride. Later, this hero’s helmsman Palinurus nods off at the rudder and tumbles overboard.
tossups.r: This hero eventually kills Turnus to win the hand of Lavinia, ending a war in Latium. For 10 points, name this Roman national epic by Virgil, which recounts the journey of a Trojan prince toward Italy.

tossups.p: This poem’s hero carries the household gods of Troy, along with his father Anchises, as he flees the city after Sinon’s wooden horse trick succeeds. Later, at Carthage, that hero’s grieving lover takes her own life with his sword atop a funeral pyre.
tossups.r: Virgil begins this poem with the line “I sing of arms and the man.” For 10 points, name this Roman epic about a Trojan refugee whose descendants go on to found Rome.

tossups.p: In this poem, the Fury Allecto helps incite a war in Italy after the hero’s son kills a tame stag belonging to a local herdsman’s daughter. This poem’s hero had earlier left the underworld through an ivory gate reserved for false dreams.
tossups.r: This poem’s hero battles Turnus for the right to marry Lavinia, daughter of King Latinus. For 10 points, name this Latin epic by Virgil, which recounts a Trojan prince’s journey toward the founding of Rome.

tossups.p: This poem’s hero marvels at a shield forged by Vulcan, decorated with scenes of Roman history including the future Battle of Actium. He receives that shield after visiting Evander at the future site of Rome.
tossups.r: This poem’s hero falls in love with Dido, the queen of Carthage, before duty calls him onward to Italy. For 10 points, name this epic poem about a survivor of the fall of Troy, written by Virgil.

tossups.p: This poem’s hero escapes the burning city of Troy carrying his father Anchises on his back and leading his young son by the hand. He later falls in love with Dido, the queen of Carthage, before leaving her to continue his journey.
tossups.r: This poem’s hero eventually settles in Italy, where his descendants will found the city of Rome. For 10 points, name this Latin epic poem written by the Roman poet Virgil.

clues.t: Latin epic poem written by the Roman poet Virgil (Publius Vergilius Maro)
Follows a Trojan prince, son of the goddess Venus and the mortal Anchises, who flees fallen Troy
Hero’s descendants become the ancestors of the Romans; written to glorify the emperor Augustus
Hero falls in love with Dido, queen of Carthage, who kills herself after he leaves her for Italy
Opens with the line “I sing of arms and the man” (Latin: “Arma virumque cano”)
Hero loses his wife Creusa while escaping burning Troy; her ghost later appears to him
Guided into the underworld in Book Six by the Sibyl of Cumae using a golden bough
In the underworld, his father Anchises shows him a pageant of future Roman heroes
In Italy, wages war against Turnus, king of the Rutulians, for the hand of princess Lavinia
The poem ends abruptly with the hero killing Turnus in single combat
Left unfinished at Virgil’s death; he had reportedly worked on it for about ten years
Modeled on Homer’s epics to give Rome its own national founding story under Augustus
Book Two: the Greek Sinon tricks the Trojans into bringing in a wooden horse; the priest Laocoon is killed by sea serpents for warning against it
Carries his father Anchises on his back and leads his son Ascanius (also called Iulus) out of burning Troy
The Harpy Celaeno curses the travelers, predicting they’ll found their city only after eating bread used as “tables”
Dido stabs herself with the hero’s own sword atop a funeral pyre after he sails for Italy
Holds funeral games in Sicily for his dead father Anchises; grieving Trojan women try to burn the fleet
His helmsman Palinurus falls asleep at the rudder and tumbles overboard; the hero later meets his ghost in the underworld
Leaves the underworld through the Gate of Ivory, reserved for false dreams, instead of the Gate of Horn
War breaks out in Italy after his son, out hunting, kills a tame stag belonging to a herdsman’s daughter
At a temple in Carthage, the hero sees a mural depicting the Trojan War, one of the poem’s famous ekphrases
Vulcan forges the hero a shield decorated with Roman history, including the future Battle of Actium
The warrior maiden Camilla is killed by Arruns, who is then struck down by Diana’s companion Opis
Enraged after recognizing the belt of his slain ally Pallas, the hero kills Turnus while Turnus wears it
Turnus’s divine sister Juturna disguises herself as a charioteer to protect him from the final duel
Dido’s dead husband Sychaeus was murdered by her own brother Pygmalion, driving her to flee Tyre and found Carthage

trap.title: The hero, or his epic?
trap.body: Quiz bowl sometimes asks for “Aeneas” (the Trojan hero) and sometimes for “The Aeneid” (Virgil’s poem about him) — they are two different answer lines, even though one real tossup on Aeneas still accepted “The Aeneid” as an alternate. A clue about the golden bough, Dido, or the fall of Troy could be building toward either one.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun. “This hero,” “this prince,” or “this man” usually wants Aeneas. “This poem,” “this epic,” or “this work” wants The Aeneid.
trap.line: Real answer line: The Aeneid (or Aeneis); a related tossup’s line: Aeneas (accept The Aeneid)
